text: The Wooden People Can Speak. Why Does the Story Still Not Treat Them as Real People?
Before people made of maize appeared, the creators had already tried more than once.
The forms made of mud could not hold together. They soon softened and fell apart.
Later, they made another set of beings out of wood.
This time, things seemed much more successful.
The wooden people had human forms. They could speak and reproduce. They lived in groups and spread across the earth. From the outside, they already did many of the “things people do.”
Yet the Popol Vuh still says: this creation failed.

The wooden people had neither minds nor hearts. They did not remember their creators and wandered without direction. Their bodies were dry, their faces lacked fullness of expression, and they could not truly understand.
Then destruction came.
A flood fell from the sky. Animals, household objects, grinding stones, cooking pots, and everything they had used also began to turn against them and accuse them.
The dogs said the wooden people never fed them, but kept beating them. Now it was the dogs’ turn to bite.
The grinding stones said they had been tormented day after day. Now they would grind the wooden people to pieces.
Pots and vessels joined the revenge.
The wooden people fled in all directions. Houses refused them shelter, trees shook them off, and caves would not let them in.
They were destroyed, and the survivors left traces in the story connecting them with monkeys.
This is not a comforting story about the creation of humanity.
It first makes the wooden people almost human, then refuses to count them as a successful creation of human beings.
Why is being able to speak not enough?
This is the first question the story puts before us.

Language is often taken as the clearest boundary between humans and other beings. The ability to express oneself in words, exchange information, and perpetuate a community seems sufficient evidence of an inner life.
But the wooden people’s speech did not bring them into genuine relationships.
The story is not simply saying that their pronunciation was inadequate.
Their problem was that they could neither remember nor respond.

They did not remember where they came from, respond to their creators, or respond to the animals and objects sharing their lives. Dogs lived alongside them, but they only used them when needed; grinding stones worked for them, but received only blows; cooking pots endured daily wear, yet never acquired any place in their world.
Language and responsiveness thus came apart.
A being can make human-sounding noises, even maintain a community, yet still make everything around it serve only its own purposes.

If it speaks only to give commands, label objects, and coordinate actions, without ever hearing through language the claims of another being, language has not automatically brought it into a shared world.
The story seems to say:
Acting like a human means more than being able to use the world.
It also means that other beings in that world can, in turn, ask something of you.
But this judgment immediately brings a danger with it.
Who has the right to declare:
You only look human, but have no real heart?
The wooden people do not write down their inner experiences for themselves. Every account of their having “no minds, no hearts, no understanding” comes from the creators and the narrator.
They have language, reproduce, and flee when destruction comes. The story describes them being pursued, struck, and rejected, yet also classifies them as a failed creation that can be discarded.
This prevents us from simply following the creators’ verdict.
If a being does not fulfill the purpose for which it was created, does its creator thereby have the right to destroy it?
An unsuccessful object can be remade.
But is a being that already speaks, avoids harm, and sustains its own life still merely a work someone has made?
When a creator says “You have no heart,” this may be a judgment about capacity.
It may also become language that makes destruction seem to need no further explanation.
Once a group is declared to lack a genuine inner life, the suffering inflicted on it can easily be treated as carrying less weight.
The story therefore leaves us with two warnings, neither of which can easily be abandoned:
Looking human does not necessarily mean possessing everything needed for a human relationship with the world.
Yet declaring a being “not enough of a real person” can itself become one of the most dangerous powers.
The wooden people’s failure was not only that they forgot their creators.

If we focus on that alone, the story can easily shrink into a lesson about obedience and gratitude: the creators gave life, so the created must remember and praise them, or their destruction is only natural.
But the counterclaims of the animals and objects make things more complicated.
The wooden people failed to respond not only upward, but also to those around them.
They lived in a world sustained by many things, yet treated all those things as silent tools.
Dogs appeared only when guarding the door or being ordered about.
Grinding stones appeared only when grain needed grinding.
Pots appeared only when food needed cooking.
They endured use, but never entered the wooden people’s memory of a shared life.
When destruction arrives, the story lets these things, always treated as voiceless, begin to speak.
This is not a conclusion, in the modern sense, that all objects have personhood.

In the narrative world of the Popol Vuh, animals, houses, and everyday implements can already participate in judgment. We cannot erase that understanding of the world and leave only an abstract definition of humanity.
Yet it still lets the reader see:
How a being treats those things that cannot respond with equal force is also part of what tells us what sort of being it has become.
Being able to speak is not the same as being able to listen.
Being able to organize life is not the same as acknowledging everything that sustains it.
Yet was the cruelty of the wooden people enough to justify the flood and their total destruction?
The story does not pause to hold a trial or give them a chance to change.
The revenge of animals and objects carries an intense pleasure of reversal: those who have long used others are at last pursued by everything they have used.
But reversal does not automatically equal justice.
The wooden people harmed the dogs. Does that mean every wooden person deserved destruction?
Was their lack of understanding their own choice, or a limitation of the creation itself?
If the creators knew that this creation had not developed the minds they expected, why destroy it outright rather than change the conditions, teach, or establish a new relationship?
These questions receive no answer in the text.
If we rush to defend the story, we make the creators’ purpose the only measure.
If we rush to portray the wooden people as a fully developed but persecuted population, we erase both the deficiencies the text repeatedly stresses and the harm they did to the beings around them.
The most honest reading can only hold both sides together:
They are not a successful creation of humanity.
But that does not automatically turn them into material that need not be taken seriously.
This story makes “What is a human being?” harder to answer than by listing capacities.
Speech is not enough.
Reproduction is not enough.
A similar outward form is not enough.
Being able to occupy land and form groups is not enough either.
But neither can we simply search for an invisible “heart” and hand the power to judge it to the strongest observer.
What deserves attention, perhaps, is whether a being can form an ongoing life, be changed by the claims of those around it, and not only use others but also let them enter its judgment.
This is still not a complete definition.
The story does not let us arrive at a definition easily.
Instead, it shows us what defining can cost:
Recognizing humanity by outward performance alone may mistake empty imitation for a human being.
Excluding beings solely by the creators’ own internal standards may, in turn, treat beings already capable of undergoing consequences as scrap.
The wooden people were ultimately classified as a failure.
Later, real people were made from maize.
This naturally encourages the reader to see the former as a stepping stone toward success: mud did not work; wood did not work; maize was finally right.
But the smoother the narrative, the more we need to stop and look at the beings left behind at the previous step.
A success story often makes earlier failures seem to exist only to serve what comes later.

Yet for the wooden people who underwent destruction, they were not “stage two in the process of making humans.” They had spoken, walked, reproduced, and sought escape when the world turned against them.
The later arrival of more complete humans does not make their destruction something that never happened.
This means the relationship between creator and creation cannot stay forever at the stage of manufacture.
When the work is still only unfeeling material, its creator can of course dismantle it and start again.
Once it has begun to sustain itself, avoid harm, and enter relationships, the creator no longer faces merely a project that falls short of a standard.
The creator faces a being whose existence has already made “failure” itself carry consequences.
The Popol Vuh does not answer for modern readers which side of the boundary of humanity the wooden people belong on.
It merely places them on that boundary in a profoundly unsettling way.
They are human enough for their destruction to disturb us.
Yet not enough like the humans the text expects for simple recognition to avoid seeming premature.
They can speak, yet have not let other voices truly enter their lives.
The creators can evaluate them, yet may also, because they hold all the power to judge and destroy, no longer need to hear those being judged.
At a certain point, then, the two sides of the story become alike:
The wooden people treat animals and objects as things solely for use.
The creators, too, may treat the wooden people as things solely for achieving their purpose of making humans.
This does not make their responsibilities the same.
But it leaves a boundary that cannot easily be crossed:
A being that never responds to the surrounding world can hardly become fully human.
And a world that acknowledges others’ place only when they meet predetermined standards has likewise not learned to respond.
The wooden people can speak.
The real question is not whether a voice has sounded.
It is who is still allowed to hear only their own voice.

*Textual basis: the creation episode involving wooden humanlike beings in the K’iche’ Maya Popol Vuh, drawing primarily on Allen J. Christenson’s parallel K’iche’–English translation. This essay retains the continuous structure in which these beings can speak and reproduce, yet are described as lacking minds and an inner center, failing to remember their creators, and facing counterclaims from animals, grinding stones, and utensils during their destruction. It does not present this particular K’iche’ narrative as a single belief shared by all Maya traditions, nor equate the wooden people directly with any modern technological system.*
